verses.translation_literal: And it happened at the double-light [noon], and Eliyahu mocked them and said: "Call out with a great voice, for a god is he! For a musing, and for a stepping-aside [to relieve himself], is to him, and a road is to him; perhaps asleep is he, and he will wake up!"
verses.translation_dramatic: At scorching high noon, Elijah began to taunt them: "Scream louder! He is a god, isn't he? Maybe he's lost in thought — or maybe he's stepped aside to use the privy! Maybe he's away on a trip, or taking a nap and waiting to be woken!"
verses.directors_commentary: Noon (tzohorayim, a dual form: "double light") is the midpoint of the Baal prophets' invocation, which began in the morning (18:26). Elijah's taunt is a run of escalating "maybe" clauses built on sound-play: ki-siach ve-ki-sig lo. The rare noun שִׂיג (sig, usually connected with the root סוג/שׂוג, "to move away, withdraw") is widely read by modern commentators as a euphemism for stepping aside to relieve oneself. The KJV's "he is pursuing" turns a crude joke into a vague errand. The polemic is precise: Ugaritic myths portray Baal as a storm god who can die, be absent from his throne and return. Those are the weaknesses Elijah mocks, during a drought that has put Baal's own speciality, rain, on trial.

philological_notes.note: Dual of tsohar, "light": noon as the doubled, brightest light of the day.
Rare verb: to mock or deceive. Elsewhere it is used of Laban cheating Jacob (Gen 31:7).
Hapax legomenon. Read as "withdrawal", and widely taken as a euphemism for going aside to defecate; paired with siach ("musing") for alliteration.

verses.translation_literal: And it happened at the going-up of the minchah, and Eliyahu the prophet drew near and said: "YHWH, God of Avraham, Yitzchak and Yisrael, today let it be known that you are God in Yisrael, and I am your servant, and by your words I have done all these things."
verses.translation_dramatic: At the hour when the afternoon offering went up, Elijah stepped up to his drenched altar. "LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel — let it be known today that you are God in Israel, that I am your servant, and that I have done all this at your word."
verses.directors_commentary: "The going-up of the minchah" is a clock reading, not a description of Elijah's sacrifice: his offering is a whole burnt offering (olah, 18:38). The afternoon minchah was offered around the ninth hour (~15:00). The KJV and the Synodal both render it "the evening sacrifice", which hides the fact that Elijah times his prayer to the hour of legitimate worship while standing in the northern kingdom. He also says "Israel" rather than "Jacob" for the patriarch, echoing the twelve stones of his rebuilt altar (18:31).

verses.translation_literal: And the hand of YHWH was upon Eliyahu, and he bound up his loins and ran before Ach'av until your-coming to Yizre'el.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the hand of the LORD seized Elijah. He hitched his robe into his belt and ran — out ahead of Ahab's chariot, through the storm, all the way to Jezreel.
verses.directors_commentary: "Binding the loins" means tucking the long tunic into the belt to free the legs. Running before a king's chariot was the job of royal outrunners (1 Sam 8:11; 2 Sam 15:1). Elijah, who has just humiliated the court's prophets, now acts as Ahab's herald, honouring the king even while opposing the king's gods. From the traditional contest site to Jezreel is roughly 25-30 km, across a valley turning to mud in the downpour.

events.title: The contest on Mount Carmel
events.narrative_summary: Elijah gathers Israel and the prophets of Baal on Carmel and proposes an ordeal: the god who answers by fire is God.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 18:1 places the word to Elijah "in the third year" of the drought; the contest follows within days. Placed 2.5 years after the oath (±0.5 year). The day starts at dawn: the Baal prophets call "from morning until noon" (18:26).
events.ancient_season_marker: End of the dry season, before the autumn rains

events.title: Elijah's challenge: "How long will you limp between two opinions?"
events.narrative_summary: Before the assembled people Elijah sets the terms of the contest; the people agree.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Opens the contest day at dawn; the speeches and the choosing of bulls take about 1.5 hours.

events.title: Elijah mocks Baal at noon
events.narrative_summary: With no answer from Baal after a morning of invocation, Elijah taunts his prophets: perhaps their god is musing, relieving himself, travelling or asleep.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 18:27 says explicitly "at noon" (batsohorayim): pinned to 12:00 on the contest day.

events.title: Fire falls at the hour of the minchah
events.narrative_summary: Elijah prays over his water-soaked altar and fire from YHWH consumes the offering, the wood, the stones and the water.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 18:36: "at the going-up of the minchah", the afternoon offering, conventionally about 15:00.

events.title: The prophets of Baal are executed at the Kishon
events.narrative_summary: The people fall on their faces confessing YHWH; Elijah has the prophets of Baal seized, taken down to the Kishon brook and killed.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Immediately after the fire; the descent from the ridge to the brook and the killing take about an hour.

events.title: Elijah prays for rain; a cloud like a man's hand
events.narrative_summary: Elijah climbs back up Carmel, crouches with his face between his knees, and sends his servant to look toward the sea seven times until a small cloud appears.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the execution the same afternoon; Ahab still has time to eat before the storm. About 30 minutes.

events.title: The drought breaks
events.narrative_summary: The sky turns black with clouds and wind, and heavy rain falls.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Starts as the servant reports the cloud; the storm lasts into the evening.

events.title: Elijah runs ahead of Ahab's chariot to Jezreel
events.narrative_summary: Ahab rides for Jezreel to beat the rain; the hand of YHWH comes on Elijah and he runs ahead of the chariot the whole way.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: About 25 km straight-line from Carmel to Jezreel. A chariot in a rain-softened valley at ~10-12 km/h needs about 2.5 hours, and a trained runner can hold that pace. Leaves around 17:00 and arrives around 19:30.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: Elijah swore there would be no rain "except by my word" (17:1); the rain returns only after his prayer on Carmel, fulfilling the terms of the oath.
The fire settles the ordeal; the people's confession gives Elijah the authority to seize the prophets of Baal.
The storm comes in direct answer to Elijah's sevenfold watch and prayer.
Ahab sets off for Jezreel "so that the rain does not stop you" (18:44): the storm sets the race in motion.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably a pun on a Phoenician cry "Where is the Prince [Baal]?", distorted in Hebrew to suggest "dung".
entities.summary_bio: Phoenician princess, daughter of Ethbaal king of Sidon, and wife of Ahab. She patronizes the prophets of Baal and Asherah and persecutes the prophets of YHWH.

entities.etymology_meaning: "Lord, owner, husband" — a title that became the name of the Canaanite storm god Hadad.
entities.summary_bio: Canaanite storm and fertility god, rider of the clouds and giver of rain in the Ugaritic texts. Promoted in Samaria under Ahab and Jezebel.
The 450 cultic prophets of Baal supported at Jezebel's table (18:19), who face Elijah on Carmel and are executed at the Kishon.

Wooded ridge running from the Mediterranean south-east toward the Jezreel Valley, on the border between Israelite and Phoenician spheres. Tradition places the contest at el-Muhraqa ("the burning") on the south-eastern summit. Coordinates are approximate.
Seasonal stream along the north-eastern foot of Carmel, draining the Jezreel Valley to the sea; also the site of Sisera's defeat (Judg 4-5).
The royal chariot in which Ahab races the storm to Jezreel. Israel was a major chariot power: the Kurkh Monolith credits Ahab with 2,000 chariots at Qarqar.
Royal city of the Omrides on the edge of the Jezreel Valley, a second residence beside the capital Samaria. Later the scene of Naboth's vineyard and Jezebel's death.

systems.name: The whole burnt offering (olah)
systems.ancient_near_east_context: The olah ("what goes up") is burnt entirely on the altar, nothing kept back for priest or worshipper. Sacrifice by fire was common across the Levant; the Carmel contest turns it into a public ordeal over which god supplies the fire.
rules_and_mechanics: An unblemished male animal is chosen.
The animal is cut in pieces and laid on wood on the altar.
The whole offering is burnt; its smoke "goes up" as a pleasing odour.

systems.name: Fire from heaven accepting an offering
systems.ancient_near_east_context: In several biblical scenes fire from YHWH ignites a sacrifice as a sign of acceptance and legitimacy (Lev 9:24; 1 Chr 21:26; 2 Chr 7:1). On Carmel the motif becomes a test of rival gods.
rules_and_mechanics: An offering is prepared without human fire.
The deity is invoked by name.
Fire consumes the offering as a public, visible verdict.

systems.name: Running before the king's chariot
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Kings and princes were preceded by runners who cleared the road and announced their arrival (1 Sam 8:11; 2 Sam 15:1; 1 Kgs 1:5).
rules_and_mechanics: Runners go ahead of the chariot on foot.
They clear the road and herald the king's approach.
Running before someone signals service and honour.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Elijah's bull, laid on an altar of twelve stones and soaked three times with water, is consumed by fire from YHWH.
system_instances.significance_note: The offering is a staged impossibility: the water rules out any trick and maximises the public proof.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Fire consumes the offering, the wood, the stones, the dust and the water in the trench.
system_instances.significance_note: Baal is the storm god of lightning; the lightning-like fire comes from YHWH instead.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Elijah runs ahead of Ahab's chariot all the way to Jezreel.
system_instances.significance_note: After defeating the king's prophets, the prophet publicly honours the king himself.

edges.description: Elijah taunts the prophets of Baal at noon over their silent god.
Elijah has the prophets of Baal killed at the Kishon brook.
Elijah runs before Ahab's chariot from Carmel to Jezreel.
